1.how: We started from the raw Xenium output of 12 brain sections, one per mouse. Each cell is a list of counts for 5,101 genes. Cells with fewer than 40 transcripts or 15 genes were removed as debris. Counts were scaled to the same total per cell and log-transformed. Cells were then grouped by similar expression with Leiden clustering, a method that finds tightly connected groups in a similarity graph. The clusters were named in three rounds. First by hand from marker genes. Then by a language model (gpt-4o-mini) given each cluster's top 20 marker genes. Then by a tool called CyteType, which wrote a finer label into a separate column. Oligodendrocyte-lineage cells were finally re-clustered on their own to split mature, immature and damaged states. There was no held-out check. The labels were judged by marker genes and by whether each class sits in the expected place in the tissue. All 12 mice were clustered together, so a disease state could form its own cluster.
1.results: QC kept 980,474 of 983,582 cells, between 69,913 and 135,378 per section. RB4403 has almost twice the cells of the others, which was later traced to over-segmentation. The final labels have 15 classes. The largest are excitatory neurons (210,407), other neurons, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes (145,940). Oligodendrocyte sub-clustering added three immature classes and a **damage-associated oligodendrocyte (DA-OL)** class of 15,261 cells. DA-OLs express stress genes (Atf4, Atf5, Gstp1), immune genes (H2-D1) and Serpina3n. They make up 64.7% of oligodendrocytes in RB4405, 42.6% in RB4627 and 21.4% in RB4401. In every other mouse they are at most 2.3%. Those three mice were later identified as the responders, so the cluster is the responder state. One caution for later runs: the class called Immature Oligodendrocytes I carries OPC markers, and no class is called OPC. The README history credits the coarse labels to CyteType. In fact they come from the language-model round.

2.how: To give every cell an anatomical region, we did not use an atlas. We clustered local tissue neighbourhoods instead. For each section, each cell's expression was added to that of its 20 nearest neighbours, which smooths out cell-to-cell noise. The pooled profiles were clustered across all sections at several resolutions. The clusters at resolution 1.0 were named by hand by comparing their position and genes with the Allen mouse brain atlas. The names were then collapsed into 12 regions such as cortex, thalamus, fibre tracts and pallidum. An earlier version based on counts of nearby cell types was dropped. All genes were used, including genes that change with disease. That choice matters later. There was no formal validation beyond visual agreement with known anatomy.
2.results: Every cell received one of 12 regions. Cortex is largest (259,386 cells), followed by thalamus (130,938), striatum and hypothalamus. Fibre tracts hold 77,564 cells and pallidum 33,663. 21,574 cells were Unknown and are left out of regional tests. The map looked anatomically sensible and was used by all regional analyses until analysis/14. **It was later corrected.** Because disease genes went into the clustering, the strong white-matter response in responders pulled pallidum into the fibre-tract label. Pallidum fell to 0-0.7% of cells in responders, against 3-7% elsewhere. A disease-free map built from anatomy-only genes fixes this (§43). The regional conclusions survive on it, but new work should use the new labels. The earlier map remains the one behind the legacy regional DE and the region x age pipeline in §8. Those results mostly blur fibre tracts and pallidum.

3.how: These were the first attempts to find what mtDSB does to the brain, run in many notebooks between autumn 2025 and early 2026. Some compared single cells of mtDSB and control mice directly. That treats thousands of cells as if they were independent replicates, which inflates significance. Later versions summed counts per mouse and cell type (pseudobulk) and used DESeq2, a count model that treats the mouse as the unit. These were run per cell type, per brain region and per induction age, P21 or P60. Some models pooled several oligodendrocyte sub-types as if they were separate mice. Others tested whether the mtDSB effect differs between ages. Gene panels for the integrated stress response (ISR) were then plotted per cell type and age. None of these runs had a control for section-level differences such as stress at sacrifice, and none checked whether every mtDSB mouse behaved alike.
3.results: The stress genes found here are real. Trib3, Gdf15, Cdkn1a, Atf5 and Serpina3n all rise in mtDSB oligodendrocytes. In mature oligodendrocytes, 4 genes passed FDR at P21 and 14 at P60. Trib3 rose about 15-fold at P21 (log2 3.89) and about 34-fold at P60 (log2 5.10), with wide error bars at both ages. From this the notebooks concluded the response is modest at P21 and strong at P60. **That conclusion did not hold.** It reflects one responder among three mice at P21 against two at P60 (§7, §9). The age model's top genes were the neuropeptides Hcrt and Pmch, which is spill-over from neurons. Many top "mtDSB genes" were section quirks: stress hormones (Sgk1, Fkbp5), Kif5a from one odd section, Il33 from one control, and Xist from sex. One note for fixing: the review document quotes the Trib3 value 5.1 ± 1.4 as P21, but it is the P60 estimate.

4.how: These models tried to respect the study's nesting: cells sit inside sections, and sections inside conditions. The main version (02/09) fitted one Bayesian model per gene on single cells. It has a baseline per cell type, a shift for mtDSB per cell type and a random effect per section. It was fitted with a fast approximate method (variational inference). The output is a posterior mean shift and a false-discovery estimate for each gene and cell type. Because there is one section per mouse, the section effect is really a mouse effect. A second version split the data by age. A third set, in PyMC, worked on per-mouse log expression. No held-out mice were used to check any of them. The goal was smaller false positives than the cell-level tests.
4.results: For oligodendrocytes, the pooled model agrees in direction with all 22 of today's driver genes it covered, 17 up and 5 down. 12 of them pass its false-discovery threshold, including Mt2, Gstp1, Atf4, Atf5 and H2-D1 up and Cldn11, Cnp and Mog down. By chance alone such agreement would happen about 2 in 10 million times. The shifts are tiny, at most 0.17 on the model's scale, because three of six mtDSB mice do not respond. The age-split version never finished: only 470 genes at P21 and 155 at P60 were read, out of 5,101. **One PyMC notebook reports the wrong number.** Its model estimates a separate level for each group, and the notebook reports the mtDSB level as if it were the effect. So "Serpina3n beta = 2.1", and the positive values for every module including myelin, are expression levels, not changes. The review and README cite this number. Serpina3n itself is confirmed elsewhere.

5.how: These runs asked whether oligodendrocytes split into normal and damaged states. Oligodendrocyte-lineage cells were re-clustered on their own, and each cluster's marker genes were read. Prespecified gene sets for progenitor, myelinating, stress, ISR and interferon states were scored in every cell. A second approach summarised each mouse's oligodendrocytes into one profile, without using group labels. It then ordered the 12 mice along a diffusion pseudotime, an ordering by gradual similarity starting from a control-like mouse. Stress and myelin scores were correlated with that order. A third run compared average counts of mtDSB and control oligodendrocytes at P60 and grouped the changed genes into functional modules. None of these used the mouse as a tested replicate. The checks came later, when each mouse was examined on its own (§7).
5.results: Sub-clustering found a distinct damage-associated cluster, DA-OL. Its markers are stress and detox genes (Gstp1, Atf4, Atf5, Car2), MHC-I genes (H2-D1, B2m) and Serpina3n. This is the same programme as the later driver genes. The P60 comparison found Trib3, Cd40, Gdf15 and Cdkn1a up 9 to 25 times in mtDSB oligodendrocytes. The myelin score was lowest in RB4405, RB4627 and RB4401, exactly the three later responders. The mouse ordering correlated with the stress score (r 0.77, p 0.003) but not with the myelin score. It mainly separated P21 from P60 mice, and its stress score included section-confound genes such as Sgk1. **The programme is confirmed.** The claim that DA-OLs appear in all mtDSB tissue is not: they appear in 3 of 6 mtDSB mice, at 21% to 65% of oligodendrocytes.

6.how: These were open-ended searches for mechanism and disease links. One notebook averaged gene-module scores over all mtDSB and all control oligodendrocyte cells. It compared them with a published pre-onset MS serum signature (IL-3, NF-kB, mitochondrial stress, myelin). Another inferred transcription-factor and pathway activity, using the decoupler tool, from the test statistics of an earlier pooled DE model. Others ran metabolic-task scoring (sccellfie), a spatial-niche method (MANA, on 250 genes) and a joint clustering with two EAE mouse datasets. The manuscript also claimed that neural stem cells near the ventricles reactivate at P60, based on legacy regional DE. None of these had a replicate-level test, and none checked whether results followed the responding mice. They were explorations rather than tests of fixed hypotheses.
6.results: Average oligodendrocyte scores were higher in mtDSB for the ISR (0.74 vs 0.59) and slightly higher for redox, glycolysis and cGAS-STING (0.080 vs 0.070). Myelin was lower (1.70 vs 1.80). The notebook read this as mtDNA leaking and triggering innate sensing, like pre-symptomatic MS. Pathway inference flagged MAPK, EGFR, p53, hypoxia and the unfolded protein response. **Most of these claims did not hold** when checked mouse by mouse (§7). cGAS-STING, NF-kB and glycolysis show no responder pattern; only Hk2 rises. The stem-cell proliferation genes are high in some controls and non-responders and follow how much ventricle each section contains. The p53 and stress-response pathway hits do fit the later ATF4 plus p53 finding (§40). The metabolic, MANA and EAE runs produced no condition-level conclusion. The MANA file holds only 250 genes and should not be used for DE.

7.how: On 14 October 2026 the classifiers showed that only three of the six mtDSB mice respond. Every earlier analysis had averaged all six against all six controls. We therefore went back through every earlier notebook, result folder and manuscript section and listed each stated conclusion. Each claim was then checked mouse by mouse. We looked up its genes in per-mouse pseudobulk profiles of oligodendrocytes, microglia, astrocytes and stem cells, in counts per million. We asked whether the effect is present only in the three responders, in all mtDSB mice, or also in some controls. A claim present only in responders is real but diluted. A claim also present in controls points to a section quirk, such as stress at sacrifice or the cutting plane. Earlier gene lists were also compared with the 34 up-regulated driver genes found later.
7.results: Ten earlier claims held, all carried by the responders. Examples: Trib3 77-214 counts per million in responders vs 1-7 elsewhere, Serpina3n 242-620 vs 34-59, and microglial Cd74 876-2705 vs 40-228. The DA-OL cluster, myelin gene loss and the thalamus and fibre-tract hotspots also held. The earlier Bayesian model agreed in direction with all 22 driver genes it covered, which we re-checked. Eleven claims did not hold. **The "P21 modest, P60 strong" story** reflects 1 responder at P21 against 2 at P60. Stress-hormone and heat-shock genes vary by section, Kif5a comes from one odd section, Il33 from one control and Xist from sex. The olfactory-astrocyte ISR, the stem-cell proliferation, cGAS-STING, NF-kB and most glycolysis genes do not follow responders. About 35 notebooks had no testable conclusion. Cataloguing found three small citation errors in the review itself.

8.how: This pipeline replaced three pasted copies of regional DE code with one tested module. For each mouse, raw counts were summed per cell type and brain region, plus one whole-section sum per cell type. These sums are called pseudobulk. Any sum from fewer than 20 cells was dropped. Within each cell type, region and age, DESeq2 compared the three mtDSB mice with the three controls. DESeq2 is a count model that treats each mouse as one replicate. A comparison was run only if each group had at least two mice. A gene counted as changed at FDR below 5%, at least a 1.4-fold change, and enough expression. A second test asked whether a region responds more than the rest of the same sections. Fake data with planted effects confirmed the code finds what it should.
8.results: 197 of 336 cell type, region and age combinations could be tested; the rest had too few cells. In total 2,024 gene changes passed. **Most are not oligodendrocyte biology.** 1,325 come from neural stem cells at P60. These reflect how much ventricle each section contains, not treatment. Hundreds more are neuronal hypothalamic peptides (Hcrt, Pmch, Pdyn) that leak into neighbouring cells. Oligodendrocytes had only 21 hits at P21 and 25 at P60. At P60, whole-section oligodendrocytes showed Mt2, Gfap, Gpnmb and Atf5 up. Big stress-gene changes such as Trib3 (16-fold) and Gdf15 (7-fold) missed significance. That is expected when three of six mtDSB mice do not respond (§10). On the later disease-free region map, total hits barely change (2,024 to 2,007).

9.how: The legacy notebooks claimed the response is weak when damage is induced at P21 and strong at P60. To test this properly, we fitted one model per cell type and region covering both ages: expression depends on age, condition, and an age-by-condition term. That last term measures how much the mtDSB effect differs between P60 and P21, and it is the one tested. Mice are the replicates, and each age-by-condition group needs at least two of them. The same significance rules as the main pipeline applied. As a cross-check, we also compared the two separate age-specific fold changes with a simple z-test. Any interaction hit was then inspected to see whether it is an oligodendrocyte gene or a neuronal transcript picked up by neighbours.
9.results: 95 of 168 cell type and region pairs had enough mice to fit. They gave 358 genes whose treatment effect differs by age. **None is an oligodendrocyte stress gene.** The 8 oligodendrocyte hits are neuropeptide and neuronal genes (Pmch, Hcrt, Gabra2), which is spill-over. Most other hits are neurons (145) and stem cells (110), which reflect section content. For the stress genes the age difference is near zero and nowhere close to significant. Gdf15 rises about 6.6-fold at P21 and 6.8-fold at P60. Trib3 rises 6.5-fold and 16-fold, but with an uncertainty that spans no difference. So there is no evidence that the response depends on induction age. The earlier impression came from having one responder at P21 and two at P60. With three mice per group, small age effects could still be missed.

10.how: We took the RNA counts of all oligodendrocytes (OLs, the myelin-making cells) in each of the 12 brain sections and summed them per section, so each mouse gave one profile. The disease-defined OL cluster was merged back into ordinary OLs first, so the clustering could not decide the answer. From the literature, before looking at the data, we fixed 10 genes that cells switch on under the integrated stress response (ISR), the alarm programme triggered by mitochondrial damage. The score is the share of OL RNA that comes from these 10 genes. A mtDSB mouse was called a responder if its score was more than 20% above the highest of the six controls. Because that rule is descriptive, we also tested the raw scores without any calling. A rank test asked whether mtDSB mice are higher on average. A variance test (Brown-Forsythe) asked whether mtDSB mice are more spread out than controls. A difference in spread with no difference in average is the signature of a group in which only some animals respond. Using a fixed gene list rules out cherry-picking genes from these same data.
10.results: Three mtDSB mice (RB4405, RB4627, RB4401) scored 1.35 to 1.57 times the highest control. The other three (RB4403, RB4630, RB4653) sat inside the control range. The group averages did not differ (p = 0.15). The **mtDSB group was about 10 times more variable** than the controls (Brown-Forsythe p = 0.0001). So half the treated mice respond strongly and half not at all. Gene by gene, seven of the ten stress genes never overlapped between responders and controls. Trib3, for example, was 77 to 214 counts per million in responders and 1 to 7 in controls. One stress gene, Psat1, actually fell in two responders. Non-responder RB4403 is slightly above the control maximum on three genes (Atf5, Ddit3, Cth), so "inside the control range on every gene" is a small overstatement. A later Bayesian model (analysis/07) put P(responder) above 0.99 for the three responders and 0.17 for RB4630, which stays borderline. A later check (analysis/15) showed responders also stand apart on microglia and on genes never used for the call, so the call is not circular.

11.how: If the responder split from the stress-gene score is real, other ways of reading the OLs should rank the same mice at the top. We compared three readouts per mouse, each built from different inputs. First, the stress-gene score from the previous run. Second, a classifier: a logistic regression trained on single OLs to tell mtDSB from control. It was run leave-one-mouse-out, meaning it was trained on the other 11 mice and then scored every OL of the mouse left out. The readout is the mouse's average predicted probability of mtDSB. This classifier never saw the disease cluster, because that cluster was merged into ordinary OLs. Third, the share of each mouse's OLs that the earlier clustering had put in the disease-associated OL (DA-OL) cluster. We then asked whether the top three mice agree across readouts and how well the readouts correlate across all 12 mice (Spearman rank correlation). Agreement between readouts that use different information argues against any one of them being an artefact of its own method.
11.results: All three readouts put the same three mice on top: RB4405, RB4627 and RB4401. By chance, the top three of 12 would all be mtDSB only 9% of the time for one readout. The classifier gave responders an average probability of 0.61 to 0.81. Controls got 0.38 to 0.60 and non-responders only 0.28 to 0.37. **22 to 65% of responder OLs fall in the DA-OL cluster**, against 0.3 to 2.3% in every other mouse. Rank correlations between readouts were 0.56 to 0.71. So the DA-OL cluster from earlier work is the responder state, and a classifier that never saw the cluster finds the same mice. The three readouts are not fully independent, because all of them come from OL RNA. The classifier is also poorly calibrated: controls score as high as 0.60, so only its ranking is meaningful.

12.how: Classifiers were trained to predict each mouse's age cohort and its treatment from its RNA. This was done per cell type and brain region, either on summed counts per mouse or on single cells. Every mouse was predicted by a model that never saw it (leave-one-mouse-out). Accuracy is the AUC, where 0.5 is chance and 1.0 is perfect. Significance came from reshuffling the labels many times while keeping the design balanced. Age works as a positive control, because the two cohorts are known to differ. We also trained on one age cohort and predicted the other. If the P60-trained model finds the P21 responder, the signature is the same at both ages. Finally we checked technical explanations for non-response: sex labels against Xist (a female-only gene, which catches sample swaps), the genotype record, the share of white matter in each section, cell counts, and which Xenium slide each mouse was on. Responders and non-responders on the same slide rule out a slide effect.
12.results: Age was easy to predict: 52 of 101 cell type by region groups were significant, and single-cell models reached a perfect AUC in 10 of 12 cell types. Treatment was not predictable anywhere: 0 of 101 groups reached p < 0.05. This follows from the responder split, since half the "mtDSB" labels belong to control-like mice. The within-cohort and cross-cohort tests compare 3 against 3 mice, so they cannot reach p < 0.05 at all. Cross-age transfer worked. **A model trained only on P60 mice ranked the P21 responder top** (0.65 vs 0.29 to 0.50), and the reverse model ranked both P60 responders top. The earlier "weak at P21, strong at P60" pattern was one versus two responders. Sex matched Xist in all 12 mice, all six mtDSB mice had the right genotype, and both slides held responders and non-responders. Age and slide are the same split, so age effects cannot be separated from slide.

13.how: We asked where in the brain the OL response sits. Each section's cells already carried a brain-region label from the original read-based region map. For every region of every mouse we computed the three readouts (stress-gene score, classifier score, disease-cluster share). Each was divided by the average of the six controls in that region, so a value of 1 means control-like. Regions with fewer than 50 OLs were left blank. Within each responder we ranked the regions from most to least affected, then averaged the ranks over the three readouts and the three responders. We also drew every OL on the tissue maps. Each OL was coloured by its classifier score or its stress-gene score, expressed as a percentile of control OLs. For the stress score each OL was averaged with its 15 nearest OLs, because single cells catch few transcripts, and compared with controls on the same slide. Sections were rotated to a common orientation so the maps can be compared. Using three readouts guards against a ranking that only one method produces.
13.results: In responders every region was affected. The stress-gene score was 1.23 to 1.88 times control, depending on region, and 21 to 65% of OLs fell in the disease cluster (controls up to 4%). **Fibre tracts and thalamus tied for the strongest response** (mean rank 2.7 of 11). Hypothalamus was mid-ranked, and hippocampus and olfactory areas were least affected. On the maps, 31 to 55% of responder OLs were above the control 90th percentile for the stress score, against 7 to 13% in controls and 8 to 14% in non-responders. They concentrate in the thalamus and the white-matter arcs. These regional differences are smaller than the responder versus non-responder difference and rest on three mice. A later check (analysis/14) found the disease had distorted the region map: pallidum had been absorbed into fibre tracts in responders. On a corrected map thalamus and fibre tracts stay on top and pallidum joins them.

14.how: We used the same single-cell classifiers as for OLs, one per cell type, to ask whether any other cell type tells mtDSB from control mice. Each mouse was predicted by a model trained on the other mice (leave-one-mouse-out). Accuracy is the AUC, where 0.5 is chance. A mouse's prediction is the average of its cells' scores, overall and per brain region. The most useful test is cross-cohort transfer: train on the six P21 mice and predict the six P60 mice, or the reverse. Transfer is harder to fool than within-cohort fits, because the model must generalise to animals on another slide. No reshuffling test was run at this level, because it would take too long on single cells. So these numbers show where to look, not proof.
14.results: Pooled across ages, no cell type predicted treatment: AUCs were about 0.5 for astrocytes, endothelial cells, microglia and OLs. Cross-cohort transfer gave weak hints. Astrocytes reached 0.78 in both directions, endothelial cells 0.78 and 1.0, and microglia 0.67 and 0.89. The endothelial P60-to-P21 model put all three P21 mtDSB mice above all three P21 controls, including the OL non-responders. The margin was tiny, though: 0.44 against 0.43. In microglia and astrocytes the P21-trained model ranked the two P60 responders highest, so microglia seem to follow the OL response. These were recorded as **hypotheses only**: no permutation test, many cell types and regions tested, and a possible artefact from controls being mounted mirror-image on the slides. A later spill-over-aware analysis (analysis/12) confirmed real changes in microglia, astrocytes and some endothelial cells of responders. It found that most neuronal hits were RNA from neighbouring cells.

15.how: We wanted the genes that make a stressed OL different from an unstressed OL in the same tissue. Comparing whole mice mixes biology with slide, section angle and time of sacrifice. Comparing cells within one section removes all of that. Every OL already had a score from the classifier: how mtDSB-like it looks, from a model that never saw its mouse. Within each section, we correlated every gene with that score across the OLs. Before looking at any genes, we fixed the rule for a "driver". The gene must correlate above 0.1 in each of the three responders, and below 0.1 on average in controls and in non-responders. The mirror rule applies to genes going down. We then grouped the drivers into programmes by hand. We measured their fold change per mouse and per region, and checked known traps. Stress-hormone (glucocorticoid) genes vary with sacrifice conditions. Genes that are mostly neuronal could be RNA leaking in from neighbouring neurons.
15.results: The rule found 34 genes going up and 9 going down. Up: the stress alarm (Atf4, Atf5, Ddit3, Trib3, Sesn2), mitochondrial and protein quality control (Hspa9, Sqstm1, Mt2), cell-cycle brakes and survival (Cdkn1a, also called p21, Ccnd1, Bcl2l1), and immune-visibility genes (H2-D1, B2m, Cd40, Serpina3n). Down: myelin genes (Cldn11, Mog, Mal, Cnp). **Six of the ten literature stress genes came back** without being given to the analysis. Per mouse, Cd40 rose from 1 to 4 counts per million to 49 to 165, while non-responders stayed flat. Stress-hormone genes had large classifier weights but no within-section signal, so they were excluded as confounds. No driver was mainly neuronal. The programme is strongest in thalamus and fibre tracts on average. It is not highest in thalamus in every responder, as FINDINGS.md says. Gene ranks rest on three mice.

16.how: With only three responders, the best check of a gene list is to see whether it reappears in completely separate animals. We trained two OL classifiers that share no mice. One learned mtDSB versus control from the six P21 mice only, the other from the six P60 mice only. Each model gives every gene a weight: positive if it pushes towards mtDSB, negative if towards control. We compared the two weight lists in two ways. First, the correlation over all 5101 genes. Second, how many genes appear in both models' top 25, 50 or 100 in each direction. The overlap was compared with what random gene lists would give (a hypergeometric test). Most genes carry no signal and add noise to the overall correlation, so the top-gene overlap is the meaningful test.
16.results: Over all genes the two models barely agreed (rank correlation 0.035), as expected when most genes are noise. Their top genes overlapped strongly. **Ten of the top 50 up-genes were shared**, where 0.5 would be expected by chance (p = 2e-11). They include the stress genes Trib3 and Atf5, Mt2 and the survival gene Bcl2l1. Four of the top 50 down-genes were shared (p = 0.001), including the myelin genes Cldn11 and Opalin. The overlap held at top 25 and top 100 for up-genes. There is a catch the notebook does not discuss. Two of the ten shared up-genes, Zbtb16 and Plin4, are stress-hormone genes that the driver analysis itself excluded as section-level confounds. Il33, among the shared down-genes, was earlier flagged as a one-control confound. So part of the replication reflects shared sacrifice or section effects, not only the mtDSB response.

17.how: We asked whether support cells next to stressed OLs react, measuring everything inside each section. For every microglia (brain immune cell), astrocyte and blood-vessel (endothelial) cell, we averaged the stress-gene score of all OLs within 50 micrometres. That gives "local OL stress". Each cell's own state was scored with gene sets fixed from the literature before the analysis. Microglia were scored for disease-associated activation (DAM), resting state, antigen presentation (MHC-I) and interferon. Astrocytes were scored for reactivity, and endothelial cells for activation. Both numbers were centred within each section and brain region. This stops regions that are high in both, such as thalamus, from creating a correlation. The correlation was computed per mouse. Controls show the baseline, since their OLs are not stressed. Responders were compared with controls by trying all 84 ways of splitting the nine mice into 3 and 6, so the smallest possible p is 0.012. The test was repeated at 30 and 100 micrometres.
17.results: Only in responders did glia track local OL stress. **Astrocyte reactivity** correlated at r 0.056 against -0.039 in controls (p = 0.012) at every radius. Microglial antigen presentation correlated at 0.031 against 0.001 (p = 0.012), and microglial DAM at 0.082 against 0.034 (p = 0.048). The resting-microglia score fell, but not significantly (p = 0.13). Endothelial cells showed nothing (p = 0.87). The correlations are small because single-cell scores are noisy, and the evidence is the consistent responder-versus-control gap. One caveat is not addressed here. The MHC-I and astrocyte gene sets include H2-D1, B2m and Serpina3n, which stressed OLs themselves switch on. RNA leaking from the OL into a neighbour could therefore inflate the effect. Later work (analysis/12) found these changes are the glia's own at the pooled level. Analysis/11 found the extra microglia are spread through white matter, not piled on stressed OLs.

18.how: All mice were sampled at one time point, so we cannot watch a cell over time. Instead we compared mice of different severity and asked how stress and myelin loss combine in single OLs. Each OL got a stress score from the 10 fixed stress genes and a myelin score from 13 fixed myelin genes. Single cells catch few transcripts, so each score was averaged with the 15 nearest OLs. It was then converted to a percentile of control OLs from the same slide and region. An OL is "stress-high" above the control 90th percentile and "myelin-low" below the control 10th. Per mouse we counted the share of OLs in each state, and the fraction of stress-high OLs that are also myelin-low. If stress comes first, mild responders should have many stressed OLs with normal myelin. With more severity, more stressed OLs should have lost myelin too. Responders were compared with controls by trying all 84 relabellings of the nine mice.
18.results: Among stress-high OLs, the share that had also lost myelin rose with severity. It was 0.40 in the mildest responder (RB4401), 0.73 in RB4627 and **0.90 in the most severe (RB4405)**, against 0.09 to 0.25 in controls (p = 0.012). In RB4401, 32% of OLs were stress-high but only 21% myelin-low. In RB4405, myelin loss (86%) went beyond the stressed cells (58%). Myelin scores fell steadily as stress rose. This fits stress coming before myelin loss, but it is a snapshot, not a time course, and the ordering rests on three mice. The excess of stressed OLs with normal myelin was not significant (p = 0.083). Non-responder RB4403 had more myelin-low OLs than controls, probably because its cells were over-split. A later count of myelin RNA without cell outlines (analysis/13) confirmed that OLs lose myelin RNA rather than disappearing.

19.how: This run asks whether a support cell's own RNA reveals how close it sits to a stressed OL, without relying on predefined gene sets. For each microglia, astrocyte and endothelial cell, we measured the distance to the nearest stressed OL. We then removed what anatomy alone explains: brain region, distance to any OL, and how many OLs are nearby. What remains is proximity to stress specifically. A ridge regression predicted this adjusted distance from the cell's full gene expression. Ridge regression is a linear model that shrinks weights to avoid overfitting. RNA from a neighbouring OL can leak into a cell's outline, so a "strict" version dropped all OL-enriched genes, all OL driver genes and the stress genes. Accuracy is the correlation between predicted and true distance in a mouse the model never saw. For responders, the model trained on two and tested on the third. Controls, trained on five and tested on the sixth, give the baseline. The responder model was also applied to controls and non-responders.
19.results: For microglia the model worked only in responders. With OL-related genes removed, the held-out correlation was 0.14 to 0.20 in responders against 0.08 to 0.13 in controls. **Every responder beat every control** (p = 0.012). The responder model did not work on controls (0.07) or non-responders (0.05). Microglia closer to stressed OLs express Cd68, Cd83 and Trem2, genes of activated, debris-eating microglia. Astrocytes showed a small but consistent excess (0.10 vs 0.09, p = 0.024). Endothelial cells showed none (p = 0.77). Controls are not at zero, because fine anatomy leaks through. Several of the top microglial weights are neuronal genes (Scn4b, Hcn1, Pde10a), so the signature is not purely microglial. The responder models also trained on fewer mice than the control models. Later work (analysis/11) found more microglia across responder white matter, not clustered on the most stressed OLs.

20.how: This run asks how many mice the next experiment needs, and which test to use. We simulated future experiments from the observed per-mouse stress-gene scores. Scores were put on a log scale and each slide's control average was subtracted. Controls were drawn from a normal distribution with the observed control spread. Each mtDSB mouse responded with probability 0.5, the observed rate, or 0.75. A responding mouse was drawn from the observed responder distribution, a non-responder like a control. We compared four tests on the same simulated data. The classic test compares group averages. A spread test (Brown-Forsythe) asks whether mtDSB mice are more variable. A responder-count test counts mtDSB mice above the control maximum, against a shuffled baseline. The last test compares averages after an induction check removes mice in which the transgene failed, assuming a perfect check. Power is the share of 600 simulated experiments that reach p < 0.05, for 3 to 12 mice per group.
20.results: Responders sit about 17 control standard deviations above controls, so each responder is obvious. The group average is still diluted by non-responders. With half the mice responding, the classic comparison had only 0.45 power at 6 mice per group and 0.69 at 12. The spread and responder-count tests reached about 0.8 at 10 mice per group. **With an induction check, 5 to 6 mice per group gave 0.80 to 0.88 power.** The recommendations are an induction check for every mouse (mtPstI qPCR or an mtDNA damage assay), per-mouse analysis, and both age cohorts on every slide. The numbers are optimistic. The parameters come from three responders and six controls. The control spread is shrunk by subtracting each slide's mean from three mice; analysis/07 gives 11 to 19 standard deviations instead. Non-responders were simulated like controls, though they vary more. The spread test's power is oddly uneven at small sizes.

21.how: We asked whether oligodendrocyte stress starts at the brain's borders, where the collaborators' staining found immune cells. Each oligodendrocyte got a stress score from a fixed list of integrated stress response genes (ISR: a cell programme switched on by damage), averaged over its 15 nearest oligodendrocytes. For every cell we measured the distance to the nearest ventricle cell, the nearest meningeal-surface cell and the nearest blood-vessel cell. Within each section we then asked whether stress falls with distance. Both stress and distance were first centred within each brain region. This matters because some regions, like the thalamus, are both more stressed and closer to certain borders, and centring stops region differences from faking a border effect. The result is one correlation per section. The unit is the mouse, since each section is one mouse. Responders were compared with controls by an exact permutation test: every possible way of choosing 3 of the 9 mice is tried, and we ask how often a random choice beats the real one.
21.results: There is no sign that stress starts at the borders. For distance to the ventricles, the correlation was 0.11 in responders and 0.04 in controls (p = 0.10). For the meningeal surface it was 0.09 against 0.02 (p = 0.25). Both are positive, so responder cells are, if anything, slightly more stressed farther from these borders. Near vessels, oligodendrocytes are slightly more stressed in all groups, including controls. That looks like normal anatomy rather than disease (p = 0.08). **The stress is a regional shift spread through the tissue**, not a front moving in from the fluid spaces or the brain surface. This is a negative result with only three responders, so a small border effect could be missed. The distances rely on the original region map, which was later corrected; this test was not re-run on the corrected map.

22.how: Here the question was whether stressed oligodendrocytes cluster into focal patches, as lesions would, or are spread evenly. We used each cell's raw stress score, with no smoothing, because averaging over neighbours would build in clustering by itself. An earlier patch analysis on smoothed scores was discarded for exactly that reason. For each oligodendrocyte we took the average stress of the other oligodendrocytes in a ring around it: 0-25, 25-50, 50-100, 100-200 and 200-400 micrometres away. This is a spatial correlogram: how strongly a cell's stress matches its neighbours' at each distance. Both values were centred within brain region, so the test asks about clustering inside a region, not the known difference between regions. That gives one correlation per section and distance ring. Responders were compared with controls using the exact permutation test over all 84 ways of picking 3 of 9 mice.
22.results: Neighbouring oligodendrocytes share stress no more in responders than in controls, at any distance. In the closest ring (0-25 micrometres) the correlation was 0.054 in responders and 0.047 in controls (p = 0.71). It stayed similar out to 200 micrometres, with all p values between 0.50 and 0.89. Only the widest ring, 200-400 micrometres, trended higher in responders (0.070 against 0.035, p = 0.08). **Stress is diffuse within regions, not focal.** Responder brains look like a uniform upward shift in thalamus and white matter rather than scattered lesions. All the correlations are small because a single-cell score from about ten genes is noisy, so weak clustering could go unseen. The test was done within regions on the original region map, so clustering that follows region boundaries is removed by design.

23.how: We asked whether the brain tries to repair damage by recruiting young oligodendrocytes near stressed ones. Immature oligodendrocytes come in three labelled types: precursor-like (type I), pre-myelinating (type II) and type III. For each immature cell we measured the average stress of oligodendrocytes within 50 micrometres. We then correlated that local stress with the cell's own proliferation, precursor and newly-formed-oligodendrocyte gene scores, within each section and after centring by region. Separately, for each mature oligodendrocyte we counted the share of immature cells within 50 micrometres and correlated it with that cell's stress. We also compared the overall share of immature cells per brain. The centring by region stops differences in anatomy from looking like local coupling. Responders were compared with controls by exact permutation, one-sided, since repair predicts an increase. Type III cells were too few in some sections and were left out.
23.results: There is no repair response at 42 days. Immature oligodendrocytes are not denser near stressed cells: the correlation was -0.007 in responders against 0.020 in controls (p = 0.98). Responder brains are not richer in them either: about 2.7 % of cells against 2.9 % in controls. Precursor-like type I cells (about 900 per section) showed no coupling to local stress, with all p values of 0.30 or more. Pre-myelinating type II cells gave a weak hint. Their proliferation and newly-formed-cell scores rose slightly with local stress in responders (both p = 0.07), but there are only about 170 such cells per section. **No detectable repair attempt** fits an early stage before the demyelination seen at 4-6 months. With three responders, a small effect could be missed.

24.how: We asked whether neurons notice the oligodendrocyte damage. Neurons near stressed oligodendrocytes might show signs of axon injury, the regeneration-associated genes switched on when axons are hurt, or their own stress response. We used four neuron classes: excitatory, inhibitory (GABAergic), medium spiny and a general neuron class. For each neuron we took the average stress of oligodendrocytes within 50 micrometres. We correlated that with the neuron's axon-injury and stress (ISR) scores within each section, after centring by brain region so anatomy cannot drive the result. That gives eight correlations per section. Responders were compared with controls by exact permutation over all 84 ways of choosing 3 of 9 mice, one-sided, since injury predicts an increase. No correction for testing eight things was applied.
24.results: Neurons near stressed oligodendrocytes show no consistent injury or stress response. For excitatory, inhibitory and medium spiny neurons, axon-injury coupling was no stronger in responders (p = 0.63, 0.70 and 0.83). Neither was stress coupling (p between 0.13 and 0.18). One test stood out: in the general neuron class, axon-injury genes rose slightly with local oligodendrocyte stress in responders. The correlation was 0.04 against -0.01 in controls, p = 0.036. That is one hit among eight uncorrected tests with a tiny effect, so it is most likely chance. However, neither the notebook text nor the README mentions it. **The overall reading is no neuronal damage yet at 42 days**, so the response stays confined to oligodendrocytes and their glial neighbours. RNA spilling between neighbouring cells could blur small effects.

25.how: Responders had been called by a hard rule: whole-brain oligodendrocyte stress above the highest control. With only three controls per slide, the control range itself is uncertain, so we gave each mouse a probability of responding instead. Each mouse's stress score was expressed relative to the average of the controls on its own Xenium slide, since the two slides differ. A Bayesian mixture model then assumes two kinds of mtDSB mouse. Non-responders look like controls, with the spread measured in controls and allowance for how few controls there are. Responders are shifted upward by an unknown amount. Because there are only six mtDSB mice, every possible split was computed exactly rather than sampled. Three checks followed. Each control was scored as if unlabelled, to show controls do not get called. Nine alternative priors (starting assumptions) were tried, to show the answer is not set by assumptions. Simulated cohorts of this design tested how often calls go wrong.
25.results: Three mice almost certainly responded: RB4627, RB4405 and RB4401 all have probability above 0.99. Their stress is 1.4-1.7 times their slide's controls, or 11-19 control standard deviations. Two almost certainly did not: RB4653 and RB4403 sit below their controls, with probability near zero. **RB4630 is the one open case at P = 0.17.** It is 1.07 times its controls, above every young control but far below any responder. Under reasonable priors it ranges from 0.01 to 0.34; a prior that cannot fit the real responders gives 0.67. No control scored as unlabelled exceeded 0.08. The estimated share of responders is 0.52, but the 90 % interval runs from 0.23 to 0.80, so six mice cannot pin it down. In simulations, true responders always got P above 0.9. Non-responders did so only 1 % of the time. **For the next cohort, stress 1.17 times the slide controls gives P of at least 0.9.**

26.how: No cluster or label in the data contains T cells, yet staining found immune cells. T cells are about 1 in 10,000 brain cells, far too few to form their own cluster among 980,000 cells. So we called them cell by cell. First we checked each lymphocyte probe on the panel: how many cells carry it and which cell types. A good T-cell probe should be rare, not spread over thousands of neurons. We then called a T cell when it had at least 3 transcripts from nine core T-cell genes (Cd3d/e/g, Cd247, Cd2, Cd8a/b1, Itk, Cxcr6), spread over at least 2 different genes. Requiring two genes rules out stray single transcripts. As a control, each gene was shuffled across the cells of its own section 20 times. This keeps how much of each gene there is but breaks which genes sit together, showing how many calls chance alone would give.
26.results: Two probes that a simple score would use are unreliable. Trbc1, part of the T-cell receptor, lights up in about 30,000 cells, 70 % of them cortical neurons. Ighm, an antibody gene, lights up in about 68,000 cells. Both carry off-target signal, and a score including Trbc1 calls about 6,000 false 'T cells'. The core genes are each seen in only 300-2,000 cells. **The co-expression rule calls 242 T cells against about 4 in the shuffled control**, roughly 60 times chance. The count is stable when the thresholds move. The called cells look like CD8 tissue-resident T cells: Cd8a/b1 with Cxcr6, Ptprc, Lck, Lat and Il7r, and little Cd4. That gives about 2.5 per 10,000 cells, ordinary for a mouse brain. Trbc1 is high inside these cells, so the probe works in real T cells but is swamped elsewhere.

27.how: With 242 T cells called, we asked what the existing annotations had called them and where they sit in the tissue. We counted their labels at three levels: the main cell class, the finer cell type and an automatic annotation. We plotted every section with its T cells marked. A T cell counted as at a border if it fell in the meninges, ventricle or vasculature regions of the original region map. To check that each call is a real cell, not a smear of transcripts from a neighbour, we drew close-ups 90 micrometres wide. These show the outline (polygon) of every segmented cell, the nucleus of the T cell, and each T-cell transcript as a dot. The two strongest T cells per section are shown in the main figure, and all 242 in a separate file. A real T cell should be small and round, with its transcripts inside its own outline.
27.results: No T cell carries a lymphocyte label at any annotation level. **They take the label of their surroundings.** 55 % sit in endothelial or leptomeningeal clusters, 18 % in astrocytes and 15 % in the stressed (DA) oligodendrocyte cluster. At the finer level, 88 are vascular leptomeningeal cells and 40 are 'mature oligodendrocytes V'. Re-clustering at any resolution scatters them over the same 2-5 large clusters. The close-ups show small round cells about 8-12 micrometres across, with the T-cell transcripts inside the outline and around the nucleus. Endothelial-labelled ones line up along vessels and the meninges, possibly still inside vessels. Oligodendrocyte-labelled ones are single cells in tissue such as striatum, hypothalamus and fibre tracts, surrounded by oligodendrocytes. One control's border label is unreliable because its region map lacks meninges under its edge.

28.how: We asked whether responder brains hold more T cells or hold them in different places, as inflammatory diseases would. For each section we counted T cells per 10,000 cells. We also counted those away from the borders (meninges, ventricles, vessels) per 10,000 cells, and the fraction away from borders. Finally we took the fraction of T cells labelled oligodendrocyte, a proxy for T cells sitting among oligodendrocytes in tissue. Each measure is one number per mouse. Responders (3) were compared with controls (6) by an exact two-sided permutation test: all 84 ways of picking 3 of the 9 mice are tried, and the smallest possible p value is 0.012. Non-responders are shown for reference but not tested. Each section holds only about 10-30 T cells, so every per-mouse fraction is coarse.
28.results: Responders do not have more T cells. They average 3.4 per 10,000 cells against 2.8 in controls (p = 0.46). The three non-responders have the fewest, 0.8-1.7. T cells inside the tissue are also not significantly more common: 1.8 against 1.2 per 10,000 (p = 0.29). The share away from borders is similar, 0.53 against 0.44 (p = 0.70). One difference came close. In two responders, RB4627 and RB4405, about 40 % of T cells are labelled oligodendrocyte, against 0-19 % in controls (group means 0.30 against 0.11, p = 0.06). The third responder, RB4401, looks like a control. RB4405 also has the most tissue T cells, 3.1 per 10,000. **mtDSB does not raise T-cell numbers.** The position hint in two mice is something to check against the staining, not evidence of T-cell damage.

29.how: Three mtDSB mice look like controls. If induction worked in only some of their oligodendrocytes, they would carry a few strongly stressed cells hidden under a normal majority. We placed each of 159,301 oligodendrocytes at its percentile among control oligodendrocytes of the same slide and brain region. Each section was left out of its own reference, so controls are scored as fairly as anyone else. Without a response, these percentiles are spread evenly. A hidden responding subset would show up as too many cells in the top 1 % or top 0.1 %. We report observed over expected, so 1.0 means no excess. This was done for the whole section and for each of six regions, to catch a local pocket. Two scores were used. The main one is the predefined stress (ISR) gene set. The second is the driver genes found earlier; those were chosen using the responders, but they still test non-responders fairly.
29.results: Non-responders look like controls at the single-cell level. With the stress score, their share of cells in the control top 1 % is 0.6-1.2 times expected, the same as controls (0.9-1.2). Responders have 5-8 times. With the driver genes, non-responders are 0.5-1.7 times, controls 0.4-2.7 and responders 15-34. **No region forms a hidden pocket.** The highest non-responder region is RB4630's fibre tracts at 1.6 times, inside what controls reach (up to 2.3). Hippocampus ratios swing because some sections hold fewer than 100 oligodendrocytes there. Responders are raised in every region, most in thalamus and fibre tracts. RB4630, the borderline mouse, sits at the top of the control range for the stress score but not the driver genes. A later robustness pass kept the responder tail result when any single responder was dropped (worst p = 0.036).

30.how: A flat tail only means something if a small responding group would have been visible. So we planted fake responding cells into control sections. First we estimated what responding cells look like from the responders' percentiles. Then we replaced 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 or 20 % of a control section's oligodendrocytes with draws from that profile, 20 times for each of six controls. A plant counted as detected if the section's top-1 % excess then beat every other control. With no cells planted, this happens 1 time in 6 by chance. Second, we estimated what share of cells respond in each mouse. A mouse's percentile distribution is treated as a mix of control-like cells, spread evenly, and responding cells. The excess in the upper tail then gives a lower bound on the responding share without assuming any shape for the responders.
30.results: The stress score would have caught a hidden responding group of about 3 % of oligodendrocytes. At 1 % planted it flagged the section 33 % of the time, at 2 % 65 %, at 3 % 98 % and at 5 % always. The driver-gene score was less sensitive here, needing 10-20 %, because one control has a high tail. In responders, **at least 20-36 % of oligodendrocytes respond** by the stress score: RB4627 36 %, RB4405 33 %, RB4401 20 %. Controls and non-responders sit at 0-7 %. By the sharper driver genes the bound is 39-79 % in responders. **So a non-responder could hide less than a tenth of the share seen in responders.** The response is all-or-none per mouse, fitting a failed induction rather than a patchy one. The 3 % limit rests on a rough model of responding cells.

31.how: Damaged oligodendrocytes in inflammatory disease are also immune-visible, so we asked whether the mtDSB response is just the generic injured-oligodendrocyte response. A public atlas of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE: a mouse model of multiple sclerosis) used the same 5,000-gene Xenium panel. That allows gene-for-gene comparison. It covers spinal cord from 8 control and 59 EAE mice across disease stages. Oligodendrocyte RNA was summed per mouse (pseudobulk) and converted to log counts per million. We computed four changes: mtDSB responders against controls on the same slide; EAE oligodendrocytes in lesions against control mice; EAE oligodendrocytes in normal-looking tissue against controls; and disease-associated against normal oligodendrocytes within EAE. Genes were kept if reasonably expressed in mtDSB oligodendrocytes, about 3,000 genes. We then compared the changes gene by gene and averaged them over gene programmes.
31.results: The two responses are only loosely related genome-wide: correlation 0.29 with EAE lesion oligodendrocytes. **The stress (ISR) and p21 / cell-cycle genes are mtDSB-specific.** Trib3 rises 5.4 log2 units in mtDSB against 0.8 in EAE lesions, and Cdkn1a (p21) 4.0 against 0.0. Averaged, the stress programme is +1.8 in mtDSB and +0.1-0.2 in EAE. **An immune-visible core is shared**: Serpina3n, Cd74, H2-D1, B2m and Hmox1 rise in both, and the immune / reactive programme is +2.3 against +2.4. EAE adds a strong interferon-gamma programme (+3.1 against +0.3) and more MHC class I (+3.3 against +0.8). Gdf15 (+4.5 against 0.0) and Eif4ebp1 fall below the expression filter, so they are missing from the saved table though the text quotes Gdf15. Brain is compared with spinal cord, and one time point with a disease course.

32.how: Pooled changes across all EAE mice could hide a single disease stage, say peak disease, where oligodendrocytes do switch on the stress response. So we scored each EAE mouse separately. For every oligodendrocyte the export script computed a stress (ISR) score: the share of its RNA from the stress genes, log-scaled. These were averaged per mouse, separately for lesions and for normal-looking tissue, keeping groups with at least 50 cells. Each mouse's average was expressed as a z-score: how many control standard deviations it sits from the control average. The mtDSB mice were scored the same way against the three controls on their own slide. The EAE mice were then laid out by disease stage, from before symptoms to remission. A stage that drives the stress response should stand out at the level of the mtDSB responders.
32.results: No EAE stage switches on the oligodendrocyte stress response at the mtDSB level. Most EAE mice sit within 2 standard deviations of the EAE controls, in lesions (average -0.3) and in normal-looking tissue (average +0.85). The three mtDSB responders sit at 4.0, 6.4 and 8.9 standard deviations above their controls; non-responders are at 0.0-1.0. However, the single highest EAE value, one peak-stage mouse in normal-looking tissue, reaches 4.1. That is just above the mildest responder, RB4401 at 4.0, so per-mouse z-scores do not fully separate the two. The scales also differ in precision, with 8 EAE controls against 3 per mtDSB slide. **The gene-level changes in the previous comparison agree**: inflammation does not drive the oligodendrocyte stress response. Some control samples carry lesion labels, an annotation oddity.

33.how: If the oligodendrocyte response is specific to mitochondrial damage, is the reaction of the surrounding glia also specific, or a common injury response? We repeated the per-mouse summed-RNA (pseudobulk) comparison for microglia, the brain's immune cells, and for astrocytes, the support cells. mtDSB responders were compared with their slide's controls. EAE cells in lesions were compared with EAE control mice. In EAE, microglia were taken from the myeloid cells annotated as microglia. We correlated the two sets of changes across all reasonably expressed genes, about 3,200-3,300 per cell type. We also averaged the change over predefined programmes. These are disease-associated microglia (DAM), homeostatic microglia genes, MHC class I, interferon and reactive astrocyte genes. This is descriptive: there is no statistical test, only side-by-side changes.
33.results: The glia react far more alike than the oligodendrocytes do. **Microglia changes correlate at 0.61 between mtDSB and EAE lesions**, against 0.29 for oligodendrocytes. The disease-associated microglia programme rises by the same amount in both, +2.6 against +2.5 log2 units. EAE microglia add more MHC class I (+2.1 against +0.8) and interferon genes (+1.4 against +0.6), and lose more homeostatic genes (-1.0 against -0.2). Astrocytes correlate at 0.43. Their reactive programme is much stronger in EAE (+3.0 against +0.8). So the glial reaction in mtDSB looks like a milder version of a common injury response, while the oligodendrocyte itself carries the distinct mitochondrial signature. The comparison is brain against spinal cord, and summed RNA from segmented cells can include RNA from neighbours.

34.how: We used all 980,474 cells from the 12 sections, each with a cell type and a region label from the original transcript-based region map. OLs and DA-OLs were counted together, because the DA-OL label partly marks responding OLs. First we checked what share of each section's cells fell in each region, to make sure every section sampled the same anatomy. Then, for each mouse, region and cell type, we computed density: cells divided by the area the region covers, measured as the number of 50 micrometre grid squares containing that region's cells. The mouse is the unit. Responders and non-responders were each compared with the six controls by an exact permutation test: every possible way of relabelling the mice is tried, and the p value is the share of relabellings giving a difference at least as large. With 3 versus 6 mice the smallest possible p is 0.012. Comparing non-responders separately rules out a generic effect of the transgene or treatment. Density, rather than share, is the main readout because a share moves whenever other cell types change.
34.results: Microglia were the one clear change. In the thalamus responders had 92-153 microglia per square millimetre against 60-82 in controls, and in fibre tracts 71-219 against 51-68. Both separate completely from controls (p = 0.012). Hypothalamus pointed the same way (p = 0.06). Cortex, striatum and hippocampus did not change, and non-responders sat inside the control range everywhere. OL density was modestly lower in responder cortex and fibre tracts (p = 0.036) with overlapping ranges. The coverage check found a surprise: **pallidum made up only 0.04-0.7 % of responder cells against 3-7 % in every other section**, while fibre tracts were larger. Neurons were also over three times denser inside responder "fibre tracts", hinting that grey matter was being labelled as white matter. Two later checks changed the picture. A disease-free region map (§43-44) showed the missing pallidum was a labelling error caused by the disease; thalamus microgliosis held there, while the fibre-tract excess weakened. The robustness pass (§47) showed this 42-test screen does not survive multiple-testing correction on its own (best q = 0.25). So the microgliosis claim rests on its replications (§35, §44), not on this screen alone.

35.how: This run repeats the microglia result without using region labels at all, because §34 raised doubts about the region map. Each section was cut into 100 micrometre squares, keeping squares with at least 20 cells. Each square was sorted by the share of its cells that are OLs, a stand-in for white matter: under 10 %, 10-30 %, 30-50 % and over 50 %. For each mouse we computed microglia per square millimetre in each class. The second part asks whether the extra microglia are dividing. A microglia counted as proliferating if it held at least one transcript of a proliferation gene such as Mki67 or Top2a. Detection depends on how many transcripts a cell has and on its region, so a logistic regression fitted on control microglia only predicted each cell's expected chance. Comparing observed with expected removes the depth and region effects. The mouse is the unit, and responders and non-responders were each compared with controls by exact permutation (smallest p 0.012).
35.results: The microglia excess appeared in OL-rich squares whatever their region label. Responders had more microglia in squares that were 10-30 % OL (p = 0.024) and 30-50 % OL (p = 0.012), and the same direction above 50 % (p = 0.08). There was no difference in OL-poor, grey-matter-like squares. **So the microgliosis is a white-matter effect that does not depend on how regions were drawn.** It was graded by mouse: RB4405 far above controls, RB4627 clearly above, RB4401 only slightly above and inside the control range in the purest white matter. One non-responder, RB4403, also had high values; the later robustness pass traced this to its over-segmentation, which doubles its cell count. In responders, 15-17 % of microglia carried a proliferation transcript against 11-15 % in controls (p = 0.012). After adjusting for depth and region the ratio was 1.17-1.23 against 0.87-1.14 (p = 0.024 from the saved table; the notebook says 0.012). Proliferating microglia per square millimetre were higher too. This supports some local proliferation, but one transcript is a weak call. Later, the label-free result held with any responder left out, while proliferation was consistent but weaker.

36.how: If stressed OLs recruited microglia one by one, the extra microglia should crowd around the most stressed OLs. Each OL got a stress percentile: where its integrated stress response score falls among OLs of the same region on the same slide in control mice, computed leave-one-out. OLs were grouped into bands: below the 50th percentile, 50-90, 90-95, 95-99 and above the 99th. For every OL we counted microglia within 50 micrometres. Within each section and region, the average count in each band was divided by the average for OLs below the median, then averaged over regions. This compares OLs in the same tissue, so differences in overall microglia density between regions or mice cancel. Controls went through the same calculation for their own top OLs. That matters because highly expressing cells tend to sit in crowded tissue, so some rise is expected even without disease. Maps of six sections showed where microglia sit.
36.results: OLs in the top 1 % of stress had only slightly more nearby microglia than unstressed OLs in the same region. In responders the ratio was 1.05-1.28, and in controls it was 0.90-1.15 for their own top OLs. Responders were not clearly above controls (p = 0.14). Non-responders ranged 0.96-1.24. **The extra microglia are spread through the affected white matter rather than piled on the most stressed cells.** This matches the earlier findings that the OL response is diffuse rather than focal and that microglial activation couples only weakly to local OL stress. The maps showed the extra microglia concentrated in the thalamus and its surrounding white matter in RB4405 and RB4627, with a dense thalamic patch in RB4405. RB4401 had a smaller patch. Whole-section numbers hide this: RB4401 had 98 microglia per square millimetre against 94 in a control. With three responders, a small focal component could still be missed.

37.how: We tested every cell type separately in responders and in non-responders against controls. The input was pseudobulk: all transcripts of one cell type in one mouse summed together, with the mouse as the unit. Differential expression used pyDESeq2 with age and group in the model. Hits needed an adjusted p below 0.05, a fold change above 1.4 and decent expression. The problem is segmentation spill-over: the imaging assigns some transcripts of a cell to its neighbours. So when OLs lose myelin RNA, every neighbouring cell type seems to lose some too. We built a simple mixing model. Marker genes expressed almost only in one cell type showed how much of each type's RNA ends up in the others. From that, and the changes measured in each source type, we predicted how much of every change in a target type is borrowed. A change was called own when borrowing explained less than half. Own changes then had to reappear in at least two brain regions, which removes effects of which regions a section contains.
37.results: Non-responders differed from controls in almost nothing: 0-4 genes in any cell type. Induction failure is therefore tissue-wide. Responders differed in every major type, most in microglia (152 genes), neural stem cells (133), endothelial cells (59) and astrocytes (45). Contamination was roughly 2-5 % of OL, microglial and endothelial RNA and 6-14 % of astrocytic RNA. **In neurons and immature OLs most hits were neighbours' RNA**: 26 of 38 neuronal hits, mostly myelin genes going "down" from OLs and Cst7 or Ccl3 going "up" from microglia. Microglia kept 135 own changes, all consistent across regions. Astrocytes kept 32, OLs 33 and endothelial cells 46, of which 25 were region-consistent. What remains is compact. Microglia show disease-associated and lipid-handling genes with growth factors and MHC. Astrocytes show reactive genes plus a type-I interferon set. Endothelial cells show a smaller interferon response. OLs keep their stress genes, which no neighbour can explain. The model is a first-order filter, and a few own calls, such as astrocyte Mbp, may still be borrowed.

38.how: The previous run left a type-I interferon programme in astrocytes. If damaged mitochondrial DNA leaked out of OLs and triggered an innate alarm, interferon-positive astrocytes should sit near stressed OLs. For each astrocyte we asked whether it carried any interferon gene transcript, such as Isg15 or Ifit1. We then computed, per mouse and region, the share of astrocytes that were interferon-positive, and compared responders and non-responders with controls by exact permutation. Within each section we also correlated interferon-positivity with two local measures: the number of microglia within 50 micrometres, and the average stress score of OLs within 50 micrometres. Both were centred within each region, so regional differences cannot drive the correlation. The local total cell count was regressed out, because crowded tissue gives every cell more neighbours and more detected transcripts.
38.results: Interferon-positive astrocytes were more frequent in responder fibre tracts (12.8-19.4 % against 7.1-10.9 % in controls) and thalamus (8.6-9.2 % against 6.6-7.7 %), both p = 0.012. But the non-responder RB4653 had the highest fibre-tract value of all, 23 %, so per region this is not a clean responder signal. Within sections, interferon-positive astrocytes were no closer to stressed OLs or to microglia than other astrocytes. All correlations stayed within plus or minus 0.03. A recomputed test on the microglia correlation gives p = 0.024 for responders, but that rests on one mouse at r = 0.03, which is negligible. **The astrocyte interferon programme is real in pooled data and is not spill-over, but it is small, patchy and not organised around the OL damage.** That contrasts with the strong interferon-gamma response seen in EAE (§33).

39.how: Neural stem cells had 133 changed genes in responders, and the manuscript claims a stem cell proliferation response. These cells live only along the ventricles, so the region check of §37 could not be applied. Different ventricles hold different stem cells: the lateral ventricle wall is a dividing niche, while the third ventricle is lined by tanycytes. If responder sections simply held more lateral ventricle, they would look more proliferative. We first read the changed genes one by one. Then we exported raw per-cell counts for selected genes. Each stem cell was marked as lateral-ventricle (Foxg1 present), third-ventricle (Tbx3 present) and proliferating (any of Mki67, Top2a, Ccnb1, Cenpf, Pcna, Mcm2, Ccna2). The key comparison is proliferation within lateral-ventricle cells only, which removes the niche difference. P21 and P60 mice were shown apart because each age sits on its own slide. Tests were exact permutations over mice.
39.results: The changed genes read as anatomy. Genes "down" in responders were third-ventricle and tanycyte markers such as Tbx3, Gpc3 and Col23a1. Genes "up" were lateral-ventricle and neurogenic genes such as Foxg1 and Erbb4, together with cell-cycle genes. Per cell this was plain. At P60, 11-14 % of control stem cells were Tbx3-positive against 0-0.7 % in the two P60 responders. The share of stem cells with a proliferation transcript did not differ (p = 0.45). **Within lateral-ventricle stem cells, responders sat inside the control range of their age** (P60 57-58 % against 52-61 %, p = 0.38). The single P21 responder was slightly high, 73 % against 44-66 %. So there is no evidence of a stem cell proliferation response. The pooled signal comes from sections that hold different ventricle walls. The manuscript's stem cell claim should be dropped or rephrased.

40.how: We asked which stress pathways mitochondrial DNA breaks switch on inside OLs. For each mouse we pooled all OL and DA-OL transcripts into one profile. Each gene's level was expressed relative to the mean of the control mice on the same slide, which removes slide effects. Eleven gene sets were fixed in advance: the ATF4 integrated stress response, p53 targets, the mitochondrial and ER unfolded-protein responses, mitophagy, mitochondrial DNA maintenance, the cGAS-STING innate DNA-sensing and type-I interferon pathway, apoptosis, senescence, the NRF2 oxidative response and cholesterol synthesis. A pathway score is the average change of its genes. Responders were compared with controls by exact permutation. Low-expressed interferon genes in OLs could be borrowed from reactive astrocytes nearby. So for every gene we used the spill-over model of §37 to estimate how much of the OL change neighbouring cells could explain.
40.results: Two pathways dominated. **The ATF4 stress response rose 1.86 log2 units and p53 targets 1.03**, while control mice stayed within about 0.2. Top genes were Trib3, Gdf15, Eif4ebp1 and Atf5, plus p21 (Cdkn1a), PUMA (Bbc3) and Gadd45a. Pro-survival BCL-XL rose and caspases stayed flat, so the cells look primed but surviving. Smaller arms rose too: Hmox1 for oxidative stress, Hspa9 for the mitochondrial unfolded-protein response, and a modest ER response. Mitophagy genes such as Pink1, Prkn and Bnip3 did not move. Senescence was partial: Serpine1 and Igfbp3 rose, but p16, Il1a and Ccl2 stayed flat. **The DNA-sensing pathway was essentially absent.** Cgas, STING, Tbk1, Irf3 and interferon-beta were flat. Small rises in Ifit1, Oasl2, Isg15 and Usp18 were on rarely expressed genes and were almost fully explained by astrocyte spill-over. Pooled data dilute the change per responding cell, so the ranking matters more than the size. All eleven pathway tests survive multiple-testing correction, and ATF4 and p53 hold with any responder left out.

41.how: The construct is driven by the Plp1 promoter, which is active in myelinating OLs. Precursor cells (OPCs) might therefore escape the damage. We exported raw per-cell counts and defined pure OPCs as precursor-cluster cells with Pdgfra transcripts and no Mog. For each cell we counted transcripts of seven stress genes (Trib3, Atf5, Ddit3, Gdf15, Sesn2, Cebpg, Cdkn1a) per 1,000 transcripts. We averaged per mouse and divided by the control mean. The same was done for mature OLs and for astrocytes. Astrocytes are the key comparison. They have no reason to switch on this OL programme, so any rise in them shows how much stressed-OL RNA leaks into neighbouring cells through segmentation. If OPCs rise only as much as astrocytes, their signal is borrowed. Responders were compared with controls by exact permutation over mice.
41.results: Mature OLs in responders carried 4.2 times the control level of stress transcripts, ranging 3.2-5.0 per mouse. Pure OPCs were at 1.19 times, close to the control maximum of 1.07. **Astrocytes, which should not respond, were at the same level, 1.21 times.** So the OPC signal matches what spill-over from nearby stressed OLs predicts, and OPCs do not mount the response themselves. That fits a construct acting in myelinating cells. Non-responders were at 1.01-1.06 in all three groups, although one non-responder had an OPC value above two responders. The OPC rise is small but consistent across responders (p = 0.024), so a very small own response cannot be fully excluded. A spared precursor pool could in principle replace damaged OLs. Whether it does needs a later time point.

42.how: Earlier myelin-gene loss was measured inside segmented cells. But much myelin RNA sits in sheaths and processes outside any cell outline: about 77 % of Mbp transcripts. Here every transcript was counted, inside or outside cells. A script read the raw transcript files for 13 genes, kept high-quality calls, and binned them on a 20 micrometre grid. The genes were myelin genes (Mbp, Mog, Mag, Cnp, Opalin, Cldn11, Ermn), OL lineage genes (Sox10, Olig2), stress genes (Trib3, Cdkn1a), the astrocyte gene Gfap and the neuronal gene Snap25. Each bin took the region of its nearest cell. Per mouse and region we computed transcripts per square millimetre and per OL. Snap25 is a negative control: it should not change. Sox10 and Olig2 test whether OLs disappear or only lose myelin genes. If OLs vanished, lineage genes per mm2 would fall; if they only lose the programme, Sox10 per OL stays flat. Responders were compared with controls by exact permutation over mice.
42.results: The myelin loss was real and not a segmentation artefact. **Mog fell 39-47 % per OL and Opalin 46-55 % in every region** (log2 -0.72 to -1.15, nearly all p < 0.05). Per square millimetre the drop was larger, because OL density also falls a little. Cldn11, Ermn and Cnp fell less. Mbp fell 16-29 % per OL and was weakest in the mildest responder, perhaps because Mbp mRNA lives long in sheaths. **Sox10 per OL did not change**, so OLs keep their identity and lose the myelin programme rather than disappearing. Olig2 per OL was flat or slightly up. Snap25 per square millimetre stayed flat. Gfap rose about 2-3 log2 units per square millimetre in thalamus, hypothalamus and fibre tracts. That shows astrocyte reactivity stronger than cell-based scores suggest, since two thirds of Gfap lies outside cells. Later checks found Mog loss holds with any responder left out, Opalin is slightly weaker, and Mbp loss rests on two responders.

43.how: The region labels came from clustering each cell together with its neighbours using all genes. In responders, stressed OLs and extra microglia could pull a region into the wrong cluster. To test this, we re-drew the map from anatomy genes that do not respond to disease. We ranked genes by how strongly they differ between regions in control mice and removed 469 known response genes: every stress, immune and myelin set, microglial markers, OL driver genes and every confirmed own change from §37. The top 400 remained. For every cell, their counts were summed with the 20 nearest cells, as in the original map. A classifier was trained on control cells with their original labels: principal component analysis followed by logistic regression. Controls are the reference because they carry no disease. It was checked by leaving one control section out at a time and predicting its labels. Then it labelled every section, and we compared the two maps.
43.results: The disease-free classifier reproduced a held-out control section's original labels for 90-95 % of cells. Most disagreements were at region borders. So the anatomy genes alone carry the region map. **In responders, pallidum came back**: RB4405 went from 0.04 % to 3.9 % of cells, RB4627 from 0.5 % to 3.3 %, and RB4401 from 0.7 % to 1.8 %. Controls sat at 2.9-4.2 %. Responder fibre tracts shrank back into the control range. Of the cells originally called fibre tract in responders, 23 % were pallidum by anatomy genes, against 4 % in controls. Outside these two regions the maps agreed about as well in responders as in controls. **So the disease, not the cutting plane, moved the white-matter-rich pallidum into "fibre tracts".** RB4401 still has somewhat less pallidum, which may be plane. Region-level work should now use the new labels, or at least treat pallidum and fibre tracts together. The region-by-age DE of analysis/01 used the old map and was re-run in §49.

44.how: Having corrected the region map (§43), we re-ran the two key regional results on both the old and the new labels side by side. The first is OL stress by region: for each mouse and region, the share of OLs above the 90th percentile of same-slide controls. Percentiles were computed leave-one-out, so a control OL is never compared with itself. The second is microglia density per region, as in §34. Eight regions were tested. Responders were compared with controls by exact permutation over mice, and each responder is shown against the control minimum-maximum range. Showing both maps side by side reveals which conclusions depended on the distorted labels and which did not. The label-free microglia result of §35 needs no re-run because it never used region labels.
44.results: The OL stress ranking held. On the new map, 28-36 % of responder thalamus OLs were above the control 90th percentile against 8-11 % in controls. Fibre tracts were at 19-33 %. **Pallidum now joined the top at 20-35 %**, having held only a few hundred responder OLs on the old map. Cortex, striatum and hypothalamus were mid-ranked, and every region was affected (p = 0.012 for most). Thalamus microgliosis was unchanged: 90-154 against 60-82 per square millimetre (p = 0.012). Hypothalamus became significant (p = 0.036). Fibre tracts weakened (p = 0.036) because RB4401 fell inside the control range; part of the old excess was pallidum. In pallidum RB4405 and RB4627 had 212 and 117 microglia per square millimetre against 62-105, but RB4401 had 62 and the test was not significant (p = 0.095). The notebook's summary calls pallidum among the strongest microgliosis regions, which overstates it. Later, 10 of these 16 regional tests survived multiple-testing correction.

45.how: The three responder mice were picked using oligodendrocyte (OL) stress genes. A sceptic could say they only look alike because of how they were chosen. To test this, we summed the RNA of each cell type per mouse (a pseudobulk) for OLs, microglia, astrocytes and endothelial cells.
