From every cell type we removed all genes that were used to call responders or to describe their OL response. For each mouse we built a profile: its expression minus the average of control mice from the same slide, leaving the mouse itself out of that average. We then correlated each mouse's profile with the average profile of the other responders. A high correlation means the mouse shares the responders' pattern. Control mice give the null, because they are compared to the same baseline and so are not exactly zero. An exact permutation test compares the 3 responders with the 6 controls: it checks every possible way of labelling 3 of the 9 mice as responders. Microglia are the key test, because no microglial gene was ever used to call responders.
45.results: In microglia, each responder correlated strongly with the other responders' profile: r = 0.57, 0.66 and 0.82. Controls ranged from -0.07 to 0.42. So the two groups did not overlap at all, which is the best possible result with these numbers (p = 0.012). This is **the cleanest independent evidence** that the three responders share a real response. In OLs with every selection gene removed, RB4405 (0.75) and RB4627 (0.57) stood well above controls, whose maximum was 0.37. RB4401 (0.37) only tied the highest control. So RB4401's OL response beyond the stress genes is weak, which fits it being the mildest responder throughout the project. Astrocytes showed a weak shared pattern (responders 0.25 to 0.44, controls 0.07 to 0.35). Endothelial cells showed none: controls reached 0.52, above all responders. Non-responders looked like controls in every cell type. The test cannot rule out a technical factor that happens to affect only the three responder sections, but the slide baseline removes slide effects.

46.how: Every per-mouse claim in the project compares 3 responder mice with 6 controls. If one responder were unusual, it alone could create a significant result. This run took 17 key per-mouse numbers from earlier analyses. They include the OL stress score, the ATF4 and p53 pathway scores, microglial activation, microglia density in several regions, and myelin RNA per OL. Two metrics were included where no change was expected (Sox10 per OL, and OPC stress at spill-over level), as negative checks. For each metric we ran an exact permutation test of responders against controls. Then we dropped each responder in turn and repeated the test with 2 responders against 6 controls. This is leave-one-responder-out: the claim must survive without any single animal. With 2 versus 6 mice the smallest possible p is 0.036, so a metric that reaches 0.036 every time is as robust as the design allows. We also checked whether each responder, on its own, lies outside the full range of the controls. For display, every value was turned into a z-score against controls from the same slide.
46.results: For 10 of the 15 metrics expected to change, the result held whichever responder was dropped (p = 0.036 every time). In all ten, each responder also lay outside the control range. These are the OL stress score, the excess of strongly stressed OLs, ATF4 and p53 pathway scores, microglial and astrocyte activation, the microglial shared profile, microglia density in thalamus and in OL-rich tissue, and Mog loss. Two metrics were consistent but weaker: proliferating microglia and Opalin per OL (worst drop-one p = 0.071). Three rest on only two responders, because RB4401 or RB4627 fall inside the control range. These are the OL signature on non-stress genes, Mbp loss and hypothalamus microgliosis (worst p 0.107 to 0.179). The negative checks behaved as expected: Sox10 per OL did not move (p = 0.89). OPC stress rose mildly (p = 0.024), at the level expected from neighbouring stressed OLs. Non-responders never differed from controls (all p of 0.27 or more). So **the core claims do not depend on any single mouse**, though the metrics are correlated and RB4401 is consistently the mildest.

47.how: Analyses 11 to 15 ran many tests at once. When you run many tests, some reach p < 0.05 by chance. False-discovery-rate control (Benjamini-Hochberg) adjusts each p-value into a q-value. A q-value below 0.10 means that, among all tests called significant at that level, at most about 10 % are expected to be false. We grouped the tests into five families, each answering one question. These were cell densities (7 cell types in 6 regions, 42 tests), regional results on the corrected region map (16), myelin transcripts per OL (13 genes in 5 regions, 65), OL pathway scores (11) and the 17 key metrics of the leave-one-out check. Correction was applied within each family, which is the stricter and more standard choice. We also pooled all 151 tests to show how much the answer depends on the grouping. Because exact tests with 3 versus 6 mice cannot go below p = 0.012, survival depends on how many tests in a family reach that floor.
47.results: Four families survived well. All 11 OL pathway scores kept q < 0.10. 45 of the 65 myelin-transcript tests did, 10 of the 16 regional tests on the corrected map, and 16 of the 17 key metrics. **The 42-test cell-density screen did not survive on its own.** Only 6 of its tests had p < 0.05. Even the two strongest, microglia in thalamus and in fibre tracts, reached only q = 0.25. So the microglia increase cannot rest on that screen. It rests instead on two separate replications, in OL-rich tissue squares and on the corrected region map, both with q < 0.10. It also rests on the leave-one-responder-out check. The modest drops in OL density in cortex and fibre tracts, and the neuron changes in that screen, should be treated as nominal hints only. When all 151 tests were pooled, the six density hits did reach q below 0.10 (0.032 to 0.066). This shows the answer depends on how families are drawn; the notebook reports the stricter within-family result.

48.how: Many notebooks read large per-cell tables that are too big or too sensitive to keep in the git repository. A new user who clones the project needs to know which files are missing and how to rebuild them. This run scanned every analysis notebook from 01 to 15. For each one it counted error messages in the saved outputs and code cells that had not been run. It then listed every untracked result file whose name appears in the notebook's code. For each such file it read the comment in the .gitignore file that explains which script recreates it. This is a bookkeeping check, not a statistical one. Its purpose is to make sure that saved figures and numbers come from complete runs, and that every hidden input has a documented recipe. It does not re-run the analyses or check that re-running gives the same numbers.
48.results: All 15 notebooks had zero error outputs. Four of them (01, 03, 05 and 07) need no hidden inputs and can be re-run from a fresh clone. The others need one or more exported tables. These are mostly the per-cell metadata and gene scores made by scripts/export_cell_table.py from the main data file on the office Mac. Others are made by the EAE export, the per-cell gene counts export, the myelin transcript export and the region x time DE script. Each one has a written regeneration note. The scan listed 6 unexecuted cells in the robustness notebook itself. This is an artefact: the scan ran while that notebook was still executing, so its own later cells had no run number yet. So **a fresh clone can open every notebook with its figures**, and re-running most of them needs the exports first. The human MS notebooks (16 and 17) were added later and are not in this table. Their inputs also come from export scripts, and the human Xenium tables are deliberately kept out of git as unpublished patient data.

49.how: The region x age analysis compares mtDSB and control mice cell type by cell type within each brain region. It sums each mouse's RNA per cell type and region (a pseudobulk) and tests each gene with pyDESeq2, a standard count-based test. An earlier check found that the original region map was distorted by the disease: in responders, part of the pallidum had been called fibre tracts. A new map, built only from anatomy genes that the disease does not change, fixed this. Here the whole region x age pipeline was re-run with the new region labels and otherwise identical settings. A gene counts as significant if adjusted p < 0.05, the fold change is at least 1.4 (|log2FC| of 0.5 or more) and expression is high enough. Like the original, this run compares all six mtDSB mice, responders and non-responders together, with controls. We then compared old and new runs in two ways. First, the number of significant genes per cell type, region and age. Second, the correlation of fold changes over genes, which shows whether the direction and size of effects stayed the same.
49.results: The total number of significant genes barely changed, from 2,024 to 2,007. Fold changes agreed closely in most regions. The median correlation across cell types was 0.95 in cortex and hypothalamus, 0.94 in thalamus, 0.93 in hippocampus and 0.92 in striatum. Agreement was lower in fibre tracts (0.87) and pallidum (0.62), the regions the correction changed. Under the old map, pallidum held almost no responder cells. The largest changes in hit counts were in striatum. For example, astrocytes at P60 went from 29 significant genes to 1, and endothelial cells from 10 to 1. So the old striatum hits partly came from tissue that had been assigned to the wrong region. Microglia in hypothalamus at P60 went the other way, from 12 to 24 genes. OLs in thalamus at P60 went from 4 to 7. So **the region x age results stand overall**, but the striatum, fibre tract and pallidum hit lists should come from the new run. A small reproducibility gap: the new run's settings file does not record that region labels were replaced; only its log does.

50.how: In the mouse, damaged-mitochondria OLs switch on a stress programme with four specific markers: TRIB3, GDF15, ATF5 and EIF4EBP1. They also switch on a more general stress arm driven by CHOP (DDIT3) and p21 (CDKN1A). OLs in the EAE mouse model of MS instead show an interferon-gamma (immune) response. Here we asked which pattern human MS OLs show. We used four public single-nucleus RNA atlases of MS brain tissue (Jäkel, Schirmer, Absinta, Lerma-Martin), 141,213 OL-lineage nuclei in total. Mouse gene names were converted to human ones. For each tissue sample and lesion type we summed the RNA of all OL nuclei (a pseudobulk), keeping samples with at least 30 nuclei. Each lesion sample was compared with the control samples of the same atlas. A gene-set score is the average change over the genes in the set. An exact permutation test compared lesion and control samples. Comparing within each atlas avoids mixing up differences in lab method between atlases. We also looked at the core genes one by one, because the core set mixes specific markers with general stress genes.
50.results: In three of the four atlases, OLs in and around MS lesions raised the mtDSB core gene set by about 0.7 to 1.2 log2 units. For example, Lerma-Martin chronic active lesions rose by 1.16 (p = 0.004). But interferon-gamma genes rose as much or more, up to 1.9 log2. In the mouse, mtDSB OLs raise interferon-gamma genes by only 0.3. Gene by gene, **the four mtDSB-specific markers were not raised** in Absinta and Lerma-Martin. TRIB3, GDF15 and EIF4EBP1 stayed within about 0.3 log2 of controls, and ATF5 was slightly down (as low as -0.80). In the mouse responders these markers rise by 2 to 5 log2. Only Schirmer showed TRIB3 and ATF5 at about +1. What rose instead was the general stress arm: CHOP by 1.0 to 2.9 log2 and p21 by 0.8 to 3.1. Jäkel, the smallest atlas, gave inconsistent results. So MS OLs look like **inflammation-exposed OLs with a CHOP / p21 stress component**, not like OLs with primary mitochondrial DNA damage. Single-nucleus data detect low-expressed genes such as TRIB3 poorly, and there are few samples per lesion type.

51.how: Summing all OLs of a sample can hide a small group of strongly affected cells. In the mouse, only a few percent of responder OLs carry the specific marker Trib3. So here we looked at single nuclei. A nucleus counted as marker-positive if it held at least two transcripts in total from the four mtDSB-specific markers (TRIB3, GDF15, ATF5, EIF4EBP1). We also counted nuclei carrying both CHOP (DDIT3) and p21 (CDKN1A), the shared stress arm. For each sample with at least 30 OL nuclei, we computed the percentage of positive nuclei, and compared lesion types with controls. In the Lerma-Martin atlas, the authors had already split OLs into published subtypes, including disease-associated ones. We scored each subtype with the same gene sets and tabulated how common each subtype is in lesions and controls. This tells us whether any known subtype corresponds to the mtDSB state. No statistical test was run on these fractions; the comparison is descriptive.
51.results: OLs carrying two or more specific-marker transcripts were **essentially absent** from three atlases. They made up 0 to 0.02 % in Absinta, 0.06 to 0.09 % in Lerma-Martin and 0 to 0.2 % in Jäkel. Lesions and controls looked the same. Only Schirmer, which has the deepest sequencing and includes cortex, detected them more often. There they made up 1.8 % in acute or chronic active lesions and 4.0 % in chronic inactive lesions, against 1.1 % in controls. OLs carrying both CHOP and p21 did rise in lesions in all three larger atlases. In Absinta they made up 0.4 to 0.5 % in lesion edges against 0 % in controls. Among Lerma-Martin subtypes, OL_Dis2 had the highest core score. It made up 4.9 % of OL-lineage nuclei in chronic active lesions against 1.3 % in controls. But its score came from the shared stress genes, not the specific markers. Single-nucleus sequencing picks up low-expressed genes less often than Xenium, so a population of 1 to 3 % could be missed.

52.how: Gene sets test a chosen handful of genes. This run asked a broader question: across all genes measured in both species, does the MS OL response look more like mtDSB or more like EAE? For each atlas and lesion type we computed how much each gene changed in lesion OLs compared with control OLs. We kept genes with reasonable expression that were also measured in the mouse comparison, about 2,100 to 2,400 genes per atlas. We then correlated these human changes with three mouse OL profiles: mtDSB responders, EAE lesions, and the disease-associated OL state seen in EAE. A Pearson correlation of 1 would mean identical patterns and 0 would mean no relation. Comparing the same human data with both mouse models in parallel shows which one it resembles more, even if both resemble it weakly. No null distribution or confidence interval was computed for the correlations.
52.results: All correlations were weak. In the three larger atlases, correlation with mtDSB ranged from 0.10 to 0.17 in most lesion types. Correlation with EAE lesion OLs ranged from 0.00 to 0.14. In all seven lesion types of Schirmer, Absinta and Lerma-Martin, the human changes correlated more with mtDSB than with EAE. The margins were small, from 0.035 to 0.16. Correlation with the EAE disease-associated OL state was about zero, apart from one negative value in Schirmer (-0.34). Jäkel, the smallest atlas, showed near-zero correlations with both models. The notebook reads the overlap with mtDSB as the shared CHOP / p21 stress arm, and the EAE-like part as the interferon-gamma programme. So the MS OL response is **a weak mix of both models, leaning slightly towards mtDSB**. Species, technology, tissue and time point all differ, which is expected to push all correlations down. Without a null distribution, the small margins should not be over-read.

53.how: Public atlases pool whole tissue blocks, so a local response in lesion OLs could be diluted. Here we used an in-house, unpublished human Xenium 5k dataset: the same spatial technology as the mouse study. It has four sections, two from MS donors and two from Baló concentric sclerosis, 274,472 cells in total. There is no pathology annotation and no control tissue, so every comparison is made within a section. OLs were identified from cell clusters expressing SOX10. Zones were drawn from the data. For every cell we measured the myelin RNA in all cells within 100 micrometres, relative to the section's well-myelinated tissue. Below 25 % of that level is demyelinated, below 60 % is edge, and above is myelinated. Neuron-rich neighbourhoods were removed as grey matter, so low myelin in grey matter is not mistaken for a lesion. We then compared OL expression in demyelinated and myelinated zones of the same section. As a spill-over control we did the same for all other cells. If neighbours rise just as much, the OL signal may be borrowed RNA rather than the OLs' own.
53.results: The main results come from the two MS sections; the Baló sections were mostly grey matter. In both MS sections, **OLs in demyelinated white matter showed the mtDSB pattern**. TRIB3 rose by 1.3 and 1.4 log2, EIF4EBP1 by 0.5 and 1.4, p21 (CDKN1A) by 1.8 and 2.3, and PUMA (BBC3) by 1.7 and 2.4. Myelin genes fell: MOG by 2.3 and 2.6, OPALIN by 2.2 and 4.2. SOX10 stayed flat, as in mtDSB mice. The edge zone was intermediate. Other cells in the same zones changed TRIB3, EIF4EBP1, p21 and PUMA little, between -0.2 and +0.4, so these rises seem OL-intrinsic. GDF15 rose in neighbours too, by 1.9 to 2.8, so its OL signal may be partly borrowed. Unlike mtDSB, lesion OLs also raised immune genes such as IRF1 and CD74. OLIG2 also fell in lesion OLs, so lineage identity rests on SOX10 alone. Zones are defined by myelin RNA, so the myelin-gene results are partly circular. The notebook text slightly understates the MOG and OPALIN drops compared with its own table.

54.how: Zone averages cannot tell whether many OLs change a little or a few change a lot, and they give no uncertainty. So here each OL was scored yes or no for carrying at least one transcript of TRIB3, EIF4EBP1, GDF15, p21 or PUMA. A combined event required one specific marker (TRIB3 or EIF4EBP1) and one p53-arm gene (p21 or PUMA) in the same cell. We compared the share of positive OLs in demyelinated and myelinated white matter as a ratio. Neighbouring cells are not independent, so we used a spatial block bootstrap. This means cutting the section into 250 micrometre squares and resampling whole squares, 300 times, to get a 95 % confidence interval. The demyelinated rim lies along the tissue edge, where cutting damage or real surface pathology could cause stress on its own. So we measured each cell's distance to the tissue border and compared OLs at different depths. Finally we repeated the comparison using only OLs more than 400 micrometres from the border, which removes the border effect.
54.results: Across all OLs, positive cells were 2.8 to 3.5 times more common for TRIB3 in demyelinated than in myelinated tissue. They were 2.8 to 2.9 times more common for p21 and 3.4 to 4.8 times for PUMA. All these confidence intervals excluded 1, so the differences are unlikely to be chance. Absolute rates were low, for example 0.7 % against 0.3 % of OLs for TRIB3. Other cells changed much less, except GDF15. **The tissue border turned out to be a real confound.** Myelinated OLs near the edge carried p21 in about 13 to 15 % of cells, against 4 % deeper in. Using only OLs deeper than 400 micrometres, demyelinated OLs still carried p21 3.1 to 3.4 times and PUMA 3.2 to 3.3 times more often. The combined marker plus p53-arm event was 3.7 and 10.5 times more common, with intervals of 1.6 to 7.1 and 3.0 to 19.6. TRIB3 alone pointed the same way (2.2 to 3.2 times) but was too sparse; its intervals included 1. These intervals reflect spatial variation within a section, not variation between donors, and there are only two donors.

55.how: Three zones are a coarse summary. If OL stress truly follows myelin loss, it should rise step by step as local myelin RNA falls. To test this without the border problem, we kept only white-matter OLs more than 400 micrometres from the tissue edge. We grouped them into seven bins of local myelin RNA, from below 15 % to above 100 % of the section's myelinated level. In each bin with at least 50 OLs, we computed the share of OLs carrying TRIB3, p21, PUMA, or the combined marker plus p53-arm event. Each MS and Baló section was plotted separately. We also drew maps of the two MS sections, showing the zones and every OL carrying the combined event. This is a descriptive analysis: no trend test or confidence intervals were computed, and no table of the binned values was saved.
55.results: The result exists only as figures, so no exact numbers can be quoted. The notebook reports that in both MS sections the share of OLs carrying TRIB3, p21 or PUMA rises as local myelin RNA falls. This holds even away from the tissue border, so it is not explained by the edge effect found earlier. On the maps, OLs carrying both a specific marker and a p53-arm gene cluster in the demyelinated rim and the edge zone next to it. Only a few sit in the myelinated interior. A **graded link between myelin loss and OL stress** fits the mouse picture, where stressed OLs lose myelin RNA. It does not show that mitochondrial DNA damage causes the human state. The myelin measure partly comes from the OLs themselves, so OLs that lose myelin RNA are partly placed in low-myelin bins by definition. The maps include cells near the border, where the stress signal is confounded. With two donors and no formal test, this should be read as a preliminary observation.
